questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.stem: A legal clerk's file note describes a court that hears appeals before the highest court.

options.text: That court is the intermediate appellate tier.
That court is a trial court of general jurisdiction.
That court is a specialized administrative tribunal.
That court is a legislative committee.

questions.explanation: The intermediate appellate tier hears appeals before the highest court. The tempting error is to confuse it with a trial court.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what a writ of mandamus compels.

answer.exemplar: A writ of mandamus compels a public official or lower court to perform a ministerial duty that the law clearly requires, when no other remedy is adequate.

questions.explanation: Mandamus compels performance of a clear ministerial duty. The tempting error is to use it to control discretionary decisions.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the scope of habeas corpus

stimulus.body: A prisoner challenges the lawfulness of detention and asks a court to order release if the detention lacks legal basis. The clerk's note must classify the remedy.

questions.stem: What remedy is described?

options.text: Mandamus, because it compels release.
An injunction, because it stops future acts.
Habeas corpus, because it tests the lawfulness of detention.
Declaratory relief, because it states rights.

questions.explanation: Habeas corpus tests the lawfulness of detention. The tempting error is to confuse it with mandamus or injunction.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A court resolves a case without trial because no genuine dispute of material fact exists. The clerk's note must label the procedure.

questions.stem: What procedure is described?

options.text: A directed verdict after trial.
A default judgment, because a party failed to appear.
A dismissal for lack of jurisdiction.
Summary judgment, because no genuine factual dispute exists.

questions.explanation: Summary judgment resolves cases without trial when no genuine factual dispute exists. The tempting error is to confuse it with a directed verdict.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks which philosophy favours broad constitutional rulings.

options.text: Judicial activism favours broad rulings.
Judicial restraint favours broad rulings.
Both philosophies favour broad rulings.
Neither philosophy favours broad rulings.

questions.explanation: Judicial activism favours broad constitutional rulings, while restraint defers to other branches. The tempting error is to reverse the labels.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of overruling a precedent
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what happens when a court overrules a precedent.

options.text: The overruled precedent remains binding on all courts.
The overrule applies only to the parties in the case.
The overruled precedent no longer controls future cases.
The overrule is void until Congress approves it.

questions.explanation: Overruling a precedent removes its controlling force for future cases. The tempting error is to assume the precedent survives.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks why a holding may be limited to its facts.

answer.exemplar: A case-specific holding resolves only the dispute before the court, so its reasoning may not automatically extend to materially different facts in later cases.

questions.explanation: A case-specific holding resolves only the dispute before the court. The tempting error is to treat every holding as a broad rule.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Law of the case on remand
questions.learningObjective: Explain law of the case on remand

stimulus.body: After an appeal, the lower court receives the case back and must follow the appellate court's prior rulings on the same issues. The clerk's note must label this doctrine.

questions.stem: What doctrine applies on remand?

options.text: Res judicata, because the case is finished.
Stare decisis, because precedent binds all courts.
Collateral estoppel, because issues are precluded.
Law of the case, because prior rulings bind the lower court.

questions.explanation: Law of the case binds the lower court to the appellate court's prior rulings on remand. The tempting error is to confuse it with res judicata.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A plaintiff sues based solely on a shared public harm common to all citizens. The clerk's note asks whether standing exists.

questions.stem: Does standing exist for a generalized grievance?

options.text: No, because a generalized grievance is insufficient for standing.
Yes, because all citizens share the harm.
Yes, if the plaintiff votes in the jurisdiction.
No, unless Congress grants a private right of action.

questions.explanation: A generalized grievance shared by all citizens is insufficient for standing. The tempting error is to assume shared harm alone suffices.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Exhaustion when the agency fails to decide
questions.learningObjective: Explain exhaustion when an agency fails to decide
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what happens to exhaustion when an agency never decides.

options.text: The plaintiff must wait indefinitely.
Exhaustion still bars suit forever.
Exhaustion is excused because the agency failed to act.
The agency's inaction is itself a decision.

questions.explanation: Exhaustion may be excused when an agency fails to decide. The tempting error is to require endless waiting.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks when a case is not moot despite the dispute ending.

options.text: When the court wants to rule anyway.
When the plaintiff changes their mind.
When the defendant apologizes.
When the issue is capable of repetition yet evading review.

questions.explanation: A case is not moot if it is capable of repetition yet evading review. The tempting error is to treat any ended dispute as moot.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply habeas corpus to pre-trial detention
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks whether habeas corpus reaches pre-trial detention.

answer.exemplar: Habeas corpus can challenge pre-trial detention when the detention lacks legal basis, though courts often defer to bail and release decisions made under proper procedures.

questions.explanation: Habeas corpus can reach pre-trial detention lacking legal basis. The tempting error is to assume it only applies post-conviction.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain mandamus limits with discretionary duties

stimulus.body: A petitioner seeks mandamus to force an official to exercise discretion in a particular way. The clerk's note must decide whether mandamus lies.

questions.stem: Does mandamus lie here?

options.text: Yes, because mandamus controls all official action.
Yes, if the petitioner shows urgency.
No, because mandamus does not control discretionary duties.
No, unless Congress authorizes it.

questions.explanation: Mandamus does not control discretionary duties. The tempting error is to use it to direct how discretion is exercised.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain summary judgment for the defendant

stimulus.body: A defendant shows that the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element of the claim. The clerk's note asks whether summary judgment is available.

questions.stem: Is summary judgment available to the defendant?

options.text: No, only plaintiffs may move for summary judgment.
Yes, but only in contract cases.
No, unless the case is frivolous.
Yes, if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element.

questions.explanation: A defendant may obtain summary judgment if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element. The tempting error is to assume only plaintiffs may move.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.learningObjective: Label a decision as activist or restrained
questions.stem: A clerk's note labels a broad ruling that overturns a statute as restrained.

options.text: The label is correct because restraint overturns statutes.
The label is correct because restraint is always broad.
The label is wrong; such a ruling is activist.
The label is meaningless because all rulings are activist.

questions.explanation: A broad ruling overturning a statute is activist, not restrained. The tempting error is to reverse the labels.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how overruling affects parties who relied on the old precedent.

options.text: Reliance interests are always ignored in overruling.
Reliance converts the precedent into a statute.
Reliance automatically blocks any overrule.
Courts may consider reliance interests when overruling.

questions.explanation: Courts may consider reliance interests when overruling a precedent. The tempting error is to ignore or overstate reliance.

provenance.author: bank-team-us-government
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks whether relief extends beyond named plaintiffs.

answer.exemplar: Relief is generally confined to the named plaintiffs, so similarly situated non-parties are not automatically covered unless they join or a class is certified.

questions.explanation: Relief is generally confined to named plaintiffs. The tempting error is to assume automatic extension to non-parties.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks whether habeas corpus reaches pre-trial detention.

answer.exemplar: Habeas corpus can challenge pre-trial detention when the detention lacks legal basis, though courts often defer to bail and release decisions made under proper procedures.

stimulus.body: A petitioner seeks mandamus to force an official to exercise discretion in a particular way. The clerk's note must decide whether mandamus lies.

questions.stem: Does mandamus lie here?

options.text: Yes, because mandamus controls all official action.
Yes, if the petitioner shows urgency.
No, because mandamus does not control discretionary duties.
No, unless Congress authorizes it.

questions.explanation: Mandamus does not control discretionary duties. The tempting error is to use it to direct how discretion is exercised.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT

stimulus.body: A defendant shows that the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element of the claim. The clerk's note asks whether summary judgment is available.

questions.stem: Is summary judgment available to the defendant?

options.text: No, only plaintiffs may move for summary judgment.
Yes, but only in contract cases.
No, unless the case is frivolous.
Yes, if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element.

questions.explanation: A defendant may obtain summary judgment if the plaintiff cannot prove an essential element. The tempting error is to assume only plaintiffs may move.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Labelling decisions as activist or restrained
questions.stem: A clerk's note labels a broad ruling that overturns a statute as restrained.

options.text: The label is correct because restraint overturns statutes.
The label is correct because restraint is always broad.
The label is wrong; such a ruling is activist.
The label is meaningless because all rulings are activist.

questions.explanation: A broad ruling overturning a statute is activist, not restrained. The tempting error is to reverse the labels.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks how overruling affects parties who relied on the old precedent.

options.text: Reliance interests are always ignored in overruling.
Reliance converts the precedent into a statute.
Reliance automatically blocks any overrule.
Courts may consider reliance interests when overruling.

questions.explanation: Courts may consider reliance interests when overruling a precedent. The tempting error is to ignore or overstate reliance.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.stem: A clerk's note asks whether relief extends beyond named plaintiffs.

answer.exemplar: Relief is generally confined to the named plaintiffs, so similarly situated non-parties are not automatically covered unless they join or a class is certified.

questions.explanation: Relief is generally confined to named plaintiffs. The tempting error is to assume automatic extension to non-parties.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Constitutional avoidance in a statutory case

stimulus.body: A court interprets a statute narrowly to avoid deciding a constitutional question. The clerk's note must label this approach.

questions.stem: What approach is described?

options.text: Constitutional avoidance, because the court sidesteps the constitutional issue.
Judicial activism, because the court rewrites the statute.
Judicial restraint, because the court defers to Congress.
Standing, because the plaintiff lacks injury.

questions.explanation: Constitutional avoidance narrows a statute to sidestep a constitutional issue. The tempting error is to confuse it with activism or restraint.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Political question and absence of a standard

stimulus.body: A court declines a case because no judicially manageable standard exists to resolve it. The clerk's note must classify the barrier.

questions.stem: What barrier is described?

options.text: Standing, because the plaintiff lacks injury.
Ripeness, because the issue is premature.
Political question, because no manageable standard exists.
Mootness, because the dispute ended.

questions.explanation: A political question exists when no judicially manageable standard exists. The tempting error is to confuse it with standing or ripeness.

questions.stem: A clerk's note asks what happens when a consent decree expires.

options.text: The decree continues indefinitely by default.
